subject: Mathematics
central_question: How can lines in three-dimensional space be described, compared and separated using direction ratios, vector equations and Cartesian equations?
in_scope_units: 11.1 Introduction: using vector algebra to study lines in three-dimensional space.
11.2 Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios of a Line: direction angles, two possible orientations and conversion between direction ratios and direction cosines.
11.2.1 Direction Cosines of a Line Passing Through Two Points: coordinate differences, distance PQ and collinearity tests.
11.3 Equation of a Line in Space: conditions that uniquely determine a line.
11.3.1 Equation of a Line Through a Given Point and Parallel to a Given Vector: vector, parametric and Cartesian forms.
11.4 Angle Between Two Lines: dot-product formula and conditions for parallel and perpendicular lines.
11.5 Shortest Distance Between Two Lines: intersecting, parallel and skew-line cases.
11.5.1 Distance Between Two Skew Lines: scalar triple-product formula in vector and Cartesian forms.
11.5.2 Distance Between Parallel Lines: perpendicular distance using a cross product.
Exercise 11.1, Exercise 11.2 and the Miscellaneous Exercise on Chapter 11.
banned_topics: Equations of planes, angles between planes and distance of a point from a plane, because no developed plane section is present in the supplied chapter text
Two-dimensional straight-line formulae as a separate topic
Vector algebra operations unrelated to forming or comparing lines
must_include_keywords: l squared plus m squared plus n squared equals 1

known_pitfalls.claim: A line has only one set of direction cosines even when no direction is specified.
known_pitfalls.correction: An undirected line has two opposite sets of direction cosines; a unique set is obtained only after choosing a direction.

known_pitfalls.claim: Direction ratios must satisfy a squared sum of 1.
known_pitfalls.correction: Direction cosines satisfy l^2+m^2+n^2=1; direction ratios only need to be proportional to the direction cosines.

known_pitfalls.claim: Any three denominators in a symmetric line equation are coordinates of a point.
known_pitfalls.correction: They are direction ratios; the point is read from the constants subtracted from x, y and z.

known_pitfalls.claim: Two lines are perpendicular whenever one pair of direction-ratio components multiplies to zero.
The shortest distance formula for skew lines can also be used unchanged for parallel lines.
known_pitfalls.correction: For parallel lines b1 cross b2 is zero, so the separate parallel-line distance formula must be used.

recommended_example_progression: Begin with NCERT Example 2 to convert direction ratios 2, -1, -2 into direction cosines.
Use NCERT Example 3 to obtain direction cosines of the line through two points.
Use NCERT Example 6 to move from point-plus-direction data to vector and Cartesian line equations.
Use NCERT Examples 7 and 8 to calculate the acute angle between lines in vector and Cartesian forms.
Use NCERT Examples 9 and 10 to distinguish shortest distance between skew lines from distance between parallel lines.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The supplied chapter contains Exercise 11.1 with Questions 1-5, Exercise 11.2 with Questions 1-15, and the Miscellaneous Exercise on Chapter 11 with Questions 1-5.
